newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. seeks info on businessman jailed in China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks info on businessman jailed in China.

text.p: The U.S. Consulate in Shanghai said on Wednesday it was seeking information from the Chinese authorities on when they would deport a U.S. businessman serving a 10-year sentence for smuggling garbage into the country.

William Ping Chen, 56, was sentenced by a Shanghai court on Monday to the jail term, deportation and a 500,000 yuan ($60,000) fine after he confessed to smuggling 238 tonnes of garbage and medical waste into Shanghai in 1995.

It was not clear when the deportation order would take effect, before or after the 10-year term. In the past, China has usually deported foreign nationals in similar situations as quickly as possible.
"We're asking for clarification on the sentence," a consulate spokesman said.

Chen's arrest was the climax of an emotional campaign launched by China in mid-1996 over illegal shipments of U.S. garbage listed as waste paper for recycling but found to contain old clothes, rubber gloves and disposable syringes.

Chen had listed the imports as waste paper and mixed paper, and proceeded with the shipments despite warnings from Shanghai environmental officials and opposition from his Chinese joint venture partners, the official Xinhua news agency said.
Xinhua said he pleaded guilty to the charges.

China used the garbage issue to whip up anti-U.S. sentiment when relations with Washington slipped over a string of disputes ranging from U.S. charges of copyright piracy in China to Beijing's anger over American support for Taiwan.
Diplomats said Chen could have been unfairly singled out by China to make a diplomatic point.

Consular officials have declined to give any details of the case or of Chen personally because of a privacy agreement signed with him. They have said Chen still has the right to appeal against the sentence.
Chen was arrested in June last year and had an open court hearing on December 2 attended by an official from the U.S. Consulate in Shanghai.

He could benefit from the warming in Sino-U.S. relations in recent months. Analysts said it would make sense to remove the garbage factor to smoothe the way for a possible visit to China in the first half of the year by U.S. Vice President Al Gore.
